correctness.rationale: For fixed d≥3 and q>q_d, Xu's Theorems 1.2–1.3 identify the stated sharp norm and sharp global squared-distance deficit in the same Fourier and surface-measure normalization. Write a=(d−1)/2 and epsilon=q−q_d. The shared periodic mean of the leading Hankel tails gives (2/pi)^(q_d/2)m(q_d)/(a epsilon), while the signed periodic difference has zero mean. Integration by parts against r^(−1−a epsilon) makes the difference continuous and Lipschitz at epsilon=0, since the differentiated integrated weight is O((1+log r)/r²), the differentiated periodic factor also has zero mean, and |x|^q log|x| is uniformly Lipschitz on bounded x for q near q_d. The Bessel remainders then have integrable logarithmic derivatives and the origin is regular. Xu's Theorem 3.9 proof, not mere positivity of fixed-cutoff sums, gives positive individual cells for q>2, including q_d. Therefore the finite-part limit along the zeros is bounded below by the first cell. Using I0=A_d/epsilon+O(1) and I0−I1=L_d+O(epsilon) gives the absolute epsilon^(1/d) law with relative O(epsilon |log epsilon|) error. Taking the quotient first gives the linear relative gap with O(epsilon²), since the common pole cancels without raising it to a varying power. The exact endpoint is unbounded. The supplied quadrature was inspected, not executed or used as an enclosure.
